extracted.intended_audience: readers of early-20th-century satirical fiction (general literary readers)
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from G. K. Chesterton's novel The Napoleon of Notting Hill — satirical, mock-journalistic prose that lampoons journalism, politics, and military posturing. The text includes embedded remarks about journalistic style and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline writing: alarm and attention-grabbing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use bold, striking headlines and posters to provoke and capture attention (examples in text: 'FROM THE FRONT. GENERAL BUCK DEFEATED. DARKNESS, DANGER, AND DEATH.'; 'WAYNE WINS. ASTOUNDING FIGHT IN THE DARK.'). The King iteratively rewrites the poster until it is 'intense enough.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make headlines large, sensational, and designed to alarm or excite readers; revise until they achieve the desired intensity. Use short, punchy lines and fear-inducing phrases. Can include speculative hooks (e.g., 'Rumoured Court-martial on General Buck.') but be mindful of libel/accuracy in a real-world context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial tone: strong, dashing, enterprising lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocate a bold, enterprising editorial voice: 'I'm going to put your paper on strong, dashing, enterprising lines.' The King explicitly wants the paper to be 'feared as well as loved.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a vigorous, theatrical tone in headlines and leading articles to project energy and influence; favor decisive rhetoric over timid or overly cautious phrasing when aiming for a flamboyant paper personality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-interest priority over individual distress
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial stance that the paper should act 'in the public interests' and 'we shall not shrink because of the distress we may cause to any individual, even the most exalted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When balancing reporting decisions, prioritize matters that serve public interest even if they harm reputations; present criticisms plainly when warranted. (This is an asserted editorial principle in the text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: avoid premature judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Even while being bold, the text counsels restraint: 'it would be premature ... to cast any reflections upon the conduct of General Buck ... give him a right to have judgment upon him at least suspended.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rushing to definitive blame or condemnation without sufficient information; signal when judgments are provisional. Balance sensational headlines with careful caveats where facts are incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match style to tempo of events (avoid ill-fitting ornament)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator notes that elaborate, romantic style is ill-suited to fast-moving war: 'War is too rapid for this style of writing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose prose style appropriate to the pace of events: employ brisk, direct reporting for rapid developments and reserve ornate metaphors for slower, reflective pieces. Using overly decorative language in urgent reporting is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strive for precise diction ('mot juste'); experiment and self-edit
rubrics_metrics.description: The manuscript shows annotations: 'Try American style', 'Good sound journalism safer', and notes about 'mot juste' — instructing the writer to seek the exact right word and to try different stylistic registers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iterate drafts in differing registers (e.g., American vs. 'good sound' journalism) and revise for the precise word choice. Encourage self-editing, side-notes, and reworking openings to find the best tone and phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use eyewitness detail and authoritative sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis on first-hand reporting and sourcing: the King wants an 'eye-witness' account; phrases like 'I have it from the front on the best authority' are used to establish credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include interviews, first-hand observations, and clearly attributed sourcing to lend authority to reports. Explicitly label eye-witness status and cite 'best authority' where available to strengthen claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sensational or rumor hooks judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: The text shows use of rumor for hooks, e.g. adding 'Rumoured Court-martial on General Buck.' to posters and copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ rumors and suggestive phrases to attract attention, but balance with sourcing and caveats (see 'premature' guidance). Sensational hooks are useful for readership but risk inaccuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual/physical presentation matters (posters, display)
rubrics_metrics.description: The King physically pastes giant wall-paper posters and enjoys the spectacle of large visible copy; presentation is used as part of editorial strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the visual display of news (poster size, placement, layout) as part of impact strategy. In print or public spaces, prominence and spectacle can amplify a message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid romanticizing mundane realities (report prosaic facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator warns against turning prosaic events into forced romance: 'that which once consisted of absurd but thrilling combats in the streets, has degenerated into something which is the very prose of warfare--it has degenerated into a siege. A siege may be defined as a peace plus the inconvenience of war.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report the factual, sometimes prosaic nature of events rather than forcing them into melodramatic narratives; resist over-romanticizing routine or drawn-out situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic persona and performative authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The King adopts the persona 'Special War Correspondent' and experiments with performative authorship and voice ('I will be an eye-witness... I leave it, Special War Correspondent of the Court Journal').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a distinctive correspondent persona can add color and authority; be consistent with the persona's voice and be transparent about its theatrical nature when necessary. Personas can be leveraged for satire or to engage readers but may blur objectivity.
